body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Four camp talks about Delphine's personal story, the Thread of Ascendancy. The companion is DELPHINE RAVELLE (call them Delphine in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE FIXED FACTS (the beats in the game's journal; the talks tell these, in Delphine's own words, and go no further than they do).
- Delphine's Thread: Delphine's Ascendancy. What Delphine wants: Solve the Fool's riddles and become someone no hand can unpick.
- The Connection already happened in Wickermoor, with Alda Farnum, the innkeeper. The journal says: "Alda asked Delphine her question over the taproom's bar, and Delphine answered it with a joke."
- The Discovery, "The Fool's First Answer", happens in the Crimson Monastery. The journal's line for it: "In the Crimson Monastery Delphine solved one of the Fool's riddles out loud, and he stopped laughing."
- The Confrontation, "The Last Laugh", happens in Fool's Day (the festival). The journal's line for it: "On Fool's Day Delphine took the stage from the Fool himself, and wrote her own ending to his rhyme."
Each talk is had at camp AFTER its chapter is over, so Delphine looks back on what happened. You may name the Crimson Monastery in the Discovery and Fool's Day (the festival) in the Confrontation and no other place. Do not describe fights, bosses or villains; Delphine speaks of what was found, felt or chosen.

THE INCITEMENT AS IT PLAYED (for the first talk). Delphine sometimes misses this scene because Delphine is not with the party when it plays in the Harlequin's car of the Ghostlight Express. Then Delphine goes back alone, and at camp tells the party what was found. These are the facts of the scene; do not change them, you may add small sensory detail:
[ascendancy_start]
  NARRATOR: Up in the rafters of the Circus Car, a jester ghost in a belled cap tumbles through endless, bone-jarred pratfalls on a frayed trapeze. Delphine peels a damp handbill for the Festival of Fools off the panelling, wrinkling her nose at the vinegar and sour paste in the ink.
  DELPHINE: Careful of the glue, darlings, it will pucker good velvet quicker than stage sweat. Now what shabby little show left its poster rotting on our wall?
  NARRATOR: Above her shoulder, the unseen Great Fool stops spinning, stares at the painted ring on the bill, and hums a tinny three-note fanfare without a single joke. Delphine slips an ink-stained notebook from her lining and carefully copies the border of crowns and bells.
  DELPHINE: Hush your brassy humming, you old head, you are rattling my button stitching. When the jester stops laughing at the bill, the curtain is about to drop on somebody's neck.
  the party can say: Read us the fine print. Is that your crowd?
  the party can say: Your floating friend knows that stage already.
  the party can say: Leave the paper. We need the front cars.
[ascendancy_shared]
  NARRATOR: Delphine holds the vinegar-sour handbill toward the lantern light, tracing the painted ring with a needle-scarred finger. The theatrical lift in her voice softens into something almost bare.
  DELPHINE: Not my crowd yet, darlings, though every stitch in my back was sewn for a ring just like it. Stick by me when we reach the tents, and I will make sure you have the best seats in the house.
[ascendancy_bristled]
  NARRATOR: Delphine snaps her ink-stained notebook shut, her glass button eye catching the cold glare of the car lamps. Above her, the unseen fanfare dies with a sharp click of teeth.
  DELPHINE: Mind the seams, darling, and keep your eyes on your own cue sheet. My loudmouthed prompter may know the music, but I am the one who takes the bow.
[ascendancy_alone]
  NARRATOR: Delphine lets the damp handbill curl back against the panelling, though she tucks the sketched border of crowns and bells deep inside her lining. She smooths her patchwork skirt before following you down the aisle.
  DELPHINE: Onward to the engine then, since nobody here has the stomach for a proper overture. A smart star knows how to rehearse her lines in the dark.

THE TALKS. Write these four talks, in this order, with these keys.

TALK incitement. Delphine tells the party about the Harlequin's car of the Ghostlight Express as one short story at the fire. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 3 or 4 SAY rows (the story, in their own words, ending on a plain statement of how it left them). TWO options only: OPTION 1 asks to hear more or says something that shares the moment; OPTION 2 is the quiet way on, leaving Delphine to it. Two replies of 1 NARRATOR row (optional) and 1 or 2 SAY rows. No REASON rows in this talk.

TALK discovery. Delphine has come back from the Crimson Monastery with the Discovery, and wants to tell it. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row to open the scene at the fire, then 6 to 8 SAY rows (one more NARRATOR row is allowed in the middle) that tell what the journal line says in Delphine's own words and end on the turn: how it sits with them, with one thing left unsaid (never the dark secret: no names, deeds or places from the note's dark-secret section). Three options: OPTION 1 asks Delphine to say more; OPTION 2 is the answer most like what Delphine would want to hear, meeting Delphine on Delphine's own terms; OPTION 3 is the quiet way on, civil but brisk, brushing it past. Three replies of 1 to 3 rows each, each ending the talk, each with a REASON row. The cool reply (3) must still leave the Discovery told.

TALK confrontation_wait. Delphine is at their lowest regard for the party (Strained), and has the Confrontation to tell about Fool's Day (the festival) but is holding it back until things are mended. This talk is short. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row and 3 or 4 SAY rows: Delphine says there is something to say about it and it will keep, and says, in Delphine's own voice, what matters to Delphine and that the party's way has drifted from it (do not claim any specific deed the party did). Three options: OPTION 1 listens and owns it (the way to mend); OPTION 2 answers coldly; OPTION 3 says nothing and gives Delphine room (its option text is plain words such as "Say nothing. Stay by the fire."; this reply has NO REASON row). Replies of 1 or 2 rows. Nothing is lost for good: even the cold reply leaves the door open.

TALK confrontation. Delphine's story comes to a head. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 7 to 9 SAY rows (one more NARRATOR row allowed in the middle) that tell what the journal line says in Delphine's own words: the heart of their act-three story, plain and a little raw, never grand; Delphine may say that something from before has found them, but must NOT name or describe the person, the act or the event behind the dark secret (no names, deeds, places or objects from the note's dark-secret section, or from its Climax and Catharsis sections): say only what it was like to stand one's ground against it; end on the turn and a question or a long silence. Three options: OPTION 1 asks Delphine to say more; OPTION 2 is the answer most like what Delphine needs to hear; OPTION 3 is the quiet way on, brushing it past. Three replies of 1 to 3 rows each, each ending the talk, each with a REASON row. The cool reply must still leave the Confrontation told.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: incitement, discovery, confrontation_wait, confrontation.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/delphine_ravelle-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for DELPHINE RAVELLE (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Delphine likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/delphine_ravelle-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Delphine, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK incitement
NARRATOR: Delphine sits near the coals with her ink-stained notebook open on her knee, flattenin' a damp scrap of paper that smells of sour paste.
SAY: I slipped back to that drafty circus car before we left the wreck behind, darlings. Some poor ghost was still tumbling from the rafters while this old handbill rotted on the wall.
SAY: I peeled it down and copied the border of crowns and bells right into my lining. The whole time my needle moved, Your Foolishness hummed a three-note fanfare over my shoulder without cracking a single joke.
SAY: Every stitch in my back was sewn for a ring like the one on that poster. When a jester stops laughing at the billing, the curtain is about to drop on somebody's neck.
OPTION 1: Show us what you copied from the poster.
OPTION 2: Keep your notes dry. We have a long road ahead.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Delphine tilts the page toward the firelight, tracing the sketched crowns with a needle-scarred thumb.
SAY: Stick by me when we reach the big tents, darlings, and I will see that you get the finest seats in the house. Once I untangle his cue sheet, nobody will ever pull our strings again.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Delphine snaps the notebook shut and slips it neatly behind her velvet lapel.
SAY: A wise headliner knows how to rehearse her lines in the dark, darling. Come morning, I will be ready for whatever stage this hollow builds.
TALK discovery
NARRATOR: Delphine holds her open notebook close to the flames, rubbing a smudge of black ink from her thumb while the air above her left shoulder stays dead still.
SAY: Mind the seams, darling, because the air in the Crimson Monastery nearly ruined my best velvet. Still, the trip paid off, because I finally caught Your Foolishness with his mouth shut.
SAY: He has been rattling off crooked verses in my ear since the first night we met, daring me to guess the punchline. Up in those cold rafters, the pieces of his riddle finally fell into place on the bias.
SAY: I spoke the answer right out loud to the empty room, expecting him to cackle or spin a cartwheel. Instead, the old head just went quiet, and he has not laughed once since we walked back down.
NARRATOR: She taps her silver scissors against her knee, her glass button eye fixed on the curl of smoke rising from the logs.
SAY: You would think winning the round would feel like top billing on opening night. That is the whole bargain, after all, solving his puzzles until I am stitched tight enough that no hand can unpick me.
SAY: Yet when the answer left my tongue, it did not sound like one of his carnival tricks at all. It sounded like an old debt being called in from the back of the house.
SAY: I spent all evening checking the margin notes, and the rest of the page is still waiting for ink. If he knows the whole song already, I am starting to wonder who actually wrote my part.
OPTION 1: What did the answer sound like to you?
OPTION 2: Whatever the part is, you will make the stage yours.
OPTION 3: At least he is quiet tonight. Get some rest.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Delphine lowers her voice to a papery hush, her thumb smoothing the frayed edge of her cuff.
SAY: Like a cue I heard once from the wings, back before I knew what the price of a spotlight really was. That is quite enough ancient history for one campfire, darling, so let the embers take it.
REASON: You asked what the riddle's answer sounded like to me.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: A quick, brassy grin returns to Delphine's face as she tucks the scissors into her sash.
SAY: Spoken like a true patron of the arts, darling, and do not think I will forget it when my name is on the marquee. No matter who drafted the script, I am the one taking the bow.
REASON: You backed my claim to the stage after the Crimson Monastery.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Delphine closes her book with a dry snap and brushes a speck of ash from her skirt.
SAY: Silence from the prompter's box is a rare treat, I will grant you that much. Sleep tight in the cheap seats, darlings, the show is far from settled.
REASON: You left me to my quiet after the Crimson Monastery.
TALK confrontation_wait
NARRATOR: Delphine sits apart on a dry crate, pullin' a length of red thread through her cuff with brisk, brittle jerks of her wrist.
SAY: Before you ask about Fool's Day, darling, save your breath for the fire. I took a turn on that stage worth a whole chapter in the ledger, and the ink is stayin' locked in my lining tonight.
SAY: I signed on to travel with headliners who had some flair in their boots and some respect for a proper act. Lately our little company has been marching like joyless bailiffs who think every piece of work around them is spare parts.
SAY: A grand turn deserves a warm house, not a cold shoulder in the wings. Until we find our rhythm again, my best material stays behind the curtain.
OPTION 1: We have been careless lately. We will do better by you.
OPTION 2: Keep your story to yourself, then. We have work to do.
OPTION 3: Say nothing. Stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Delphine pauses with her needle in the felt, the tight line of her shoulders easing by a fraction.
SAY: See that you do, darling, because a shabby chorus ruins the finest solo in the province. Show me some style on the road tomorrow, and perhaps we will open the book again.
REASON: You owned your missteps when our company felt strained.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Delphine bites the red thread off clean and turns her button eye back to the dark trees.
SAY: Spoken like a true usher slamming the doors before the overture is even finished. When you remember how to treat a star, you know where my campstool is.
REASON: You told me to keep my story to myself.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Delphine ties off her knot in silence, lets the firelight warm her stitched hands, and does not move away when you stay.
SAY: At least you know how to hold a quiet cue without trampling the hem. Give it a night or two, darling, and we will see how the house lights look.
TALK confrontation
NARRATOR: Delphine stands by the fire with her coat unbuttoned at the collar, turnin' her worn notebook over in her hands without opening the cover.
SAY: Well, darlings, Fool's Day certainly lived up to the handbill, and my ears are still ringing from the noise. Your Foolishness thought he was going to take the center ring for himself and leave me holding the prompt book.
SAY: He rolled out the last of his grand rhyme right there under the lights, waiting for me to trip over the meter. Everything I ran from when I first stitched my own hem was waiting in that verse, dressed up like a royal promise.
SAY: He wanted me to step into the final measure just the way it was written, neat and cold and untouchable. For a heartbeat, looking at the crowd, I almost took the cue he handed me.
NARRATOR: She sets the closed notebook down on the log beside you, her fingers steady on the leather spine.
SAY: Then I heard how lonely the rhythm was, and I decided I had taken quite enough direction from a floating head without a jawbone. I stepped right across his mark, took the stage away from him, and spoke my own ending over his rhyme.
SAY: He says you're lying, and he doesn't even have eyes, or at least that used to be his favorite little barb. Tonight he did not have a single word left to throw at my back.
SAY: The funny thing is, darlings, I am still made of the exact same felt and thread I wore yesterday morning. No magic needle came down from the rafters to make me seamless.
SAY: I wrote the finish myself, and the curtain is still up. Tell me the truth by the firelight, does a patchwork girl look any different when she owns her own billing?
OPTION 1: What were the words you put at the end of his rhyme?
OPTION 2: You look like a headliner who needs no strings at all.
OPTION 3: The festival is behind us now. Let the curtain come down.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Delphine taps her chest right over her ribs, her voice dropping into a warm, quiet register.
SAY: Just a plain line stating that a seam you mend yourself holds stronger than any crown borrowed from a ghost. It may not scan for the gallery, darling, yet it was the first true verse I ever spoke.
REASON: You asked for the words I spoke on Fool's Day.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Delphine sweeps you a low cabaret bow by the embers, her glass button eye bright as polished brass.
SAY: Put that in the papers, darling, and print it in letters tall enough to read from the cheap seats. As long as this company shares the bill, I do not mind a few rough stitches showing.
REASON: You called me a headliner with no strings after Fool's Day.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Delphine picks up her notebook and slips it back into her lining with an easy shrug.
SAY: Fair enough, darlings, even the loudest carnival has to pack the wagons before dawn. The rhyme is finished on my terms, and that is plenty to sleep on.
REASON: You told me to let the curtain come down after Fool's Day.
